This item is for defence production, which covers a very broad field. I want to refer briefly to the statement by the minister thig afternoon that in the allocation of contracts for the expenditure of money for the purposes of this vote the great potential for the manufacture of munitions was in Ontario and Quebec. If that is the thinking of the department, that is the way the money will be spent under this item. I disagree with that statement. While the minister indicated this afternoon that he has done some pretty broad and comprehensive planning in the mechanics he has set up in his department, that particular statement is not correct in the light of the defence program. The great potential for munition making under present circumstances, and as we see a potential war developing, is not in the centre of Canada. In my opinion the major portion of the armed force we are building today is designed for western Europe. The whole program of arming our north Atlantic pact countries means that the munitions and equipment necessary for that purpose will have to be shipped to Europe, so the logical place to do the manufacturing is the point closest to Europe. Even though you now have an overdeveloped fabricating organization in the two central provinces, the great bulk of the raw materials are being dragged here from the east coast. That seems pretty illogical, and it tends to great waste if you haul your raw materials all the way up here, manufacture them and then haul them all the way back to the east coast again and ship them overseas from Halifax or Sydney. If the minister is realistic, as I know he is-though he may have some bad advisers who have centralized minds-he will agree with me.
Then I am convinced that this is not a short range program. This program is going to last for a long time. I believe in connection with munitions and vehicles, if you like, the minister should think in terms of allocating a large plant as near basic steel as he can get it, and in an area where labour is available. The hon. member for Royal has indicated, and he is quite right, that the greatest export from the maritimes is our young people. We have all the ingredients necessary for an economic program in connection with munitions, vehicles and things of that kind, which will have to be shipped out of the country; and they should be produced as close to the sources of raw material and labour as you can get. If this were a war we would be getting over in three or four years and we had an emergency program it would be all right to throw up your plants anywhere, as was done during the last war; but that is not the case. In my opinion this is a long range, more or less permanent

program; and if the money of the taxpayers is to be fairly allocated in view of economic conditions the minister should give serious thought to the establishment of a plant or two in the area where both raw materials and shipping facilities are available.
I would like the minister to think of that, because as I see our program developing today the thinking is exactly the same as it was during the last war, when we overdeveloped industry in the central provinces, particularly in Ontario, to such an extent that a power shortage was created. That power shortage still exists, so that Ontario now is racing around the country asking for a billion dollar expenditure in the St. Lawrence so they can get more power to meet a potential industrial development in this province that is not warranted. I am leaving that thought with the minister, because certainly this is not an equitable development. I believe it is uneconomic and shortsighted, and it is not like the minister to carry on a program of that kind. I wish he would take that question under advisement. I do not believe it is good thinking to centralize everything in these two provinces, with the chance of an atomic bomb wiping out everything overnight. It is still early; this program is just getting started; it is still in the embryo stage. So I hope the minister and his advisers will sit down and seriously consider utilizing, in the part of the country where they are located, the raw materials that are being dragged across this country for fabrication.
Most of the stuff we are going to manufacture will be sent to Europe, as I have said. Having that in mind, the closest you can get to raw materials, shipping facilities and a labour supply is down on the east coast, so I leave that thought with the minister. If I had been here when the first item was called I might have developed a real argument, but I am rather restricted now. I suggest that the minister think over my observations and let us know what can be done.

I want to be quite fair in this, Mr. Chairman, and I know the minister will appreciate that. I am just hoping that after I am through the minister will promptly

make a statement to the house, and to the country, respecting this important industry at Sarnia where this blast occurred. It was perhaps a miracle in many ways that it did not do more damage. I have some questions to ask the minister concerning this particular explosion. I believe the public is rather unfortunately informed about what took place, because I am inclined to believe that some of the statements that were carried in the press and over the radio were exaggerated. Perhaps this was due to the fact that statements were not immediately forthcoming from either the minister or the top management at Sarnia.
Living on the border as I do, I know that our people listen to the United States radio stations. One of them thought that this was an atomic explosion. I believe the people in Sarnia are most fortunate that it was not worse than it was. It was disastrous enough. I noticed a statement made by the minister that the damage was from $50,000 to $100,000. He may revise that statement. I think it was made immediately after the explosion. What concerns me and the people in my area, which is a chemical valley, is an article which appeared in the magazine published by the Polymer employees. The minister in his statement after the explosion did say that there had been two previous explosions. I want the members of the committee to appre-[DOT] ciate the fact that the minister did state at that time that this particular element, butadiene, is not one of the easiest elements to handle. What disturbs so many people, apparently, is the fact that there were not two but three previous explosions, I believe, in that particular area.
Hon. members may not realize it but this tank was made of steel seven-eighths of an inch thick. Of course all the plate glass windows in the neighbourhood were blown out, and fragments of steel pipe were found a mile or a mile and a half from the scene of the explosion. I am also informed-and I think this will impress upon the committee just how serious the explosion was-that one fitting or valve weighing 26J pounds was found a little more than a mile and a half away from the explosion. I should now like to pay a tribute to those in Polymer and to the fire department who played such an heroic part in averting What could have been much more serious.
I am now going to quote an article which appeared in the official staff publication of the Polymer Corporation. The quotation I hold in my hand was taken from tlje Canadian Observer, which in turn took it from an article which appeared in the company publication. It is dated Monday, May 7, 1951. It
Supply-Defence Production refers to an explosion in March of this year, or an averted one. It says:
A potentially serious fire at Polymer corporation's butadiene extraction unit was averted on March 29, through the bravery of an operating crew, according to a graphic story appearing in the latest edition of the "Polysphere," official staff publication of the crown company.
Then it goes on to speak about the heroes and says:
With absolute disregard for their personal safety, these men prevented what could have been a serious fire March 29 by shutting off escaping butadiene which was being released to the atmosphere through a ruptured butadiene product line.
The article continues:
At approximately 4.25 p.m. on March 29, a 6-inch steel line connecting three butadiene accumulators ruptured, releasing approximately 9,000 pounds of butadiene to the atmosphere. The line ruptured with considerable report, bringing the operating crew to the scene immediately.
Because of the dense hydrocarbon fog which enveloped the area, it was impossible to determine where the leak was coming from.
Then it goes on to speak about how three of the employees shut off the plug valves, and how McEachran, Moore and Roberts entered the dense hydrocarbon fog and tried to shut off one 6-inch plug valve, but found that they could not.
That to me is disturbing, and it is also disturbing to the people in my area. It may be that an inquiry has been held to determine why that valve could not be shut off at that time. These are elements so peculiar in their nature that we can think of explosive qualities in many of the products coming from a chemical valley.
The article continues:
They shut off the plug valve at a header which shut off the violently roaring hydrocarbon, thus stopping the leak and giving them a chance to see the source of the leak.
The last paragraph reads:
Cause for the line rupturings was attributed to a formation of "popcorn" which develops when pure butadiene remains dormant in a line for long periods of time. It is a risk common to industries where butadiene is used1.
In one of his previous statements the minister emphasized that. I have practically every article that appeared in the press at London, Windsor, Sarnia, Toronto and so on. I am not going to deal with them in detail. I think the committee is already impressed with what happened and with what was averted. If I were speaking on civil defence I would go into it in greater detail, and I will at a later time; for what happened that night was almost a calamity because of the thousands of cars which gathered in a very few minutes.
I am going to bring my remarks to a close with some questions which I should

Supply-Defence Production like to have the minister answer, perhaps not tonight, but at any time that he feels so disposed. The people are entitled to it. I was hoping that an inquiry would have been held into this explosion immediately and the public properly informed of what actually happened. I was there for two days after the explosion. I did not want to bring it up at that time because I thought that I would give it more thought, and I did not want to create any commotion. Under these conditions perhaps we have to accept the unusual and take it in our stride.
There is another reference here by a former employee who dealt with an explosion earlier, and maybe at some later date I will go into it. There is some question about the statement of this particular employee who attended at a previous explosion. What alarms us down there is this. This plant is adjacent to the Imperial Oil Company refinery, which is the largest refinery in the British empire, and which is now increasing its production by about 25 per cent. Just on the other side of Polymer is the Dow chemical plant, another chemical industry. They all play an important part in our war potential.
Apparently the so-called "popcorn" is something that accumulates in a line. The minister can correct me if I am wrong, but I understand there were four explosions within eleven months, or three averted explosions. I should like to know what this so-called "popcorn" element is, and how it forms in this particular line. How rapidly does it build up? If it does build up, why is it not removed periodically? Can it form a plug in the line? It apparently did because there was notice to the people in that area that something serious was happening. A flare showed ten times as bright for two or three moments, and then shut off. Apparently the escape valve did not work. Could it form a plug in the line? Was the line failure caused by excessive pressure? Was the six-inch line of adequate strength to withstand anticipated pressure? Was the line seamless or welded? Could the line have been weakened by corrosion or other causes? If the line plugged up could the butadiene build up enough pressure to rupture the line? Are there safety valves which shut off the flow of butadiene when the pressure increases above normal operating pressure? Are those safety valves tested periodically to determine if they operate satisfactorily? There is evidence to which I have already referred that they do not operate.


Have there been other cases where similar failures have occurred in installations handling butadiene? If not, how have they been prevented?
The crew was unable to close the six-inch plugged valve. Was the plugged valve damaged by a line rupture or was it out of order because of failure to lubricate it, or for some other reason? Would a gate valve have been easier to close?
I am referring to the explosion on Sunday, May 6, 1951. I am asking if there was an investigation after the line rupture on March 29. Were any steps taken to instal safety devices and prevent further failure? Were the 30,000-gallon tanks and connecting lines of adequate strength for the anticipated pressure? Was this tank normally used for butadiene storage? Could popcorn have formed and plugged some of the equipment or the pressure release line? How did the butadiene ignite?
Those are the questions, Mr. Chairman. I doubt if the minister will be able to answer them immediately. However, I think that it may be that inquiries by those competent to make them could find some reason for this occurrence. It might have been a spark or flame in the area. Theories have been advanced. For instance, did butadiene in the line and tanks have oxygen mixed with it to form an inflammable mixture? What amount ' of oxygen or air is required to form an explosive mixture with butadiene?
I intended to be brief, and I hope I have been fair. I believe I would not do justice to the constituency I represent if, in the light of what took place, I failed to ask the minister for an explanation. I know some of these questions are technical, and if he is not prepared to answer them tonight it will be satisfactory if they are answered at a later date.
I should like hon. members to appreciate that those of us in that area were greatly concerned, and we were much relieved that the explosion did not do more damage. I am hopeful that we will not have three or four explosions in a year, and I am sure that with the able direction available in the Polymer Corporation management that will not take place.
I know they are working with a dangerous element. Hon. members will appreciate that in the chemical industry there is a constant fight with treacherous elements. I trust the minister will take my remarks in the spirit in which they are offered, and make some explanation to the committee.

I never attempted to minimize the seriousness of the explosion which took place recently. But I think it is a remarkable tribute to the safety precautions taken at the plant that an explosion of that magnitude could happen without loss of a life, and with only very limited damage to property. I am told the damage has now all been repaired and that section of the plant is operating again at full capacity.
The plant was built by experienced chemical engineers, and it was designed in units to minimize damage from explosion. speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The function of Canadian
Arsenals Limited is to operate stand-by arsenal capacity in time of peace, and to keep the arsenals in readiness to expand in time of war; and the corporation has been carrying out that function. The purpose in establishing the arsenals after the war was to have in them capacity for making anything Canada made during the last war; and all the arts of the last war have been preserved in the arsenals.
The Quebec arsenal is making shell cases, filling shells, and making the various components of explosive charges. It is carrying out a pretty well rounded program in the field of ammunition. St. Paul l'Ermite was a shell filling plant in the last war and it is handling the same work at the present time. It is filling shells made at various arsenals other than the Quebec arsenal. The Longueuil plant was equipped with finishing machinery for artillery, horizontal boring machines and machinery taken from a number of gun plants built and operated by private firms during the last war. It was a well rounded plant in finishing capacity, but it had no primary capacity. On the other hand Sorel, a much larger plant, had primary capacity and some finishing capacity, but both were out of

balance if operated separately. After a good deal of study our officers decided to combine the two plants and use the excess primary capacity of Sorel with the finishing capacity of Longueuil. That seems to have worked out very well, and additional production will be possible as a result of the combination of the two plants.
Then we have Valley field, which was an explosives plant dealing with various kinds of nitrocellulose powder, TNT and various other explosives. That plant was kept in a standby position in peace. When defence production became necessary it required a good deal of rehabilitation, and Defence Industries Limited have been retained on a management contract to put the plant in shape and bring it back into production. The Lindsay arsenal is operating as it has always operated, making shell casings and shells of various calibres, mainly the larger ones. Then coming into the Toronto area a portion of the former Research Enterprises Limited is now a branch of Canadian Arsenals which is being expanded to take over a part of the radar program. It is the nucleus of the production of early warning radar sets. The small arms division in the Toronto area is the focal point for the production of small arms. At the moment it is tooling up for 50 millimetre aircraft guns, and as soon as we determine the type of rifle to be produced it will go back into the manufacture of rifles and automatic weapons.

DEPARTMENT OF TRADE AND COMMERCE General administration-
449. Departmental administration, $513,280.
Is the minister prepared to make a statement on our trade position now?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Yes, I shall be glad to make a statement. I will try to keep it a little shorter than the one on defence production. During this session there have been several opportunities to discuss the activities of the Department of Trade and Commerce. We have had a debate on the Torquay trade agreements. Legislation has been brought down amending the Weights and Measures Act, which is administered by this department. During the debate on the speech from the throne I also gave a review of the work of the department. The committee will recall that wheat policy,

Supply-Trade and Commerce and the activities of the Canadian wheat board, have come in for extensive discussion from time to time during the past few months. It is hardly necessary, therefore, for me to give a lengthy statement at this time.
I would like, however, to offer a few comments on Canadian trade policy. Since the end of the war very great efforts have been made by the government, and the Department of Trade and Commerce in particular, to enlarge the volume of Canadian trade. These efforts have taken many forms. The trade commissioner service abroad has been strengthened. Canada has supported international action to reduce trade barriers. When this country was suffering from a serious shortage of dollars, the government did everything possible to encourage exports to dollar areas and to encourage imports from soft currency countries. The establishment of the international trade fair in 1948 was another evidence of the government's interest in an expanding volume of trade, both import and export.
The efforts have borne fruit. Canada's trade has expanded to an extent that few thought possible. It is in better balance visa-vis the dollar and sterling areas. The position now, however, is very different from what it has been in these last few years. We are once again in a seller's market, faced with the fact or the prospect of shortages of certain materials because of the competing demands of the defence program. In the light of this change in the trade outlook, the government has reviewed its policy to see whether the emphasis on trade is misplaced.
We have come to the conclusion that while the needs of defence are paramount, Canada continues to have a vital interest in foreign trade. The defence program, and the high rate of consumer and business spending which accompanied it, have resulted in a high level of imports. These imports must be paid for. For that reason alone we cannot afford to neglect our export trade. But there is a longer-run reason as well. All of us hope and believe that the present emergency will pass. In so far as possible, therefore, trade contacts should be retained and developed, looking to the time when Canada will once again have to seek out buyers for its surpluses.
Accordingly, as I said at the opening of the international trade fair in Toronto this year:
There is to be no general let-down in our efforts to promote export trade. That is the policy of the Department of Trade and Commerce and of the Canadian government. We are having special supply difficulties to meet in various lines of export business. We shall probably continue to have such difficulties. But the fact that we shall be giving first

priority to defence production needs is not to be taken to mean that the servicing of our export business will be pushed into the background or left without the very closest attention that we can give it.
In May the United Kingdom-Canada continuing committee on trade and economic affairs met in Ottawa. As was announced at the time, the United Kingdom hopes to buy a very much increased volume of goods in Canada during the next year. We, for our part, are anxious that the United Kingdom and the sterling area generally should continue to ship as much as possible to Canada. The discussions were most useful, and it is our hope that they will result not only in a substantial increase in the volume of United Kingdom-Canada trade but in further progress towards the restoration of normal trading relationships between the sterling area and Canada, which is our ultimate goal.
The United Kingdom talks were immediately followed by discussions with the British West Indies. There have always been close commercial ties between Canada and the British West Indies, and the imposition of restrictions upon imports from Canada into these islands had undoubtedly been the cause of a good deal of inconvenience and disruption to both importers and exporters. The introduction of the trade liberalization plan at the beginning of this year was an important step forward, and we are hopeful that it will be followed in the near future by further progress in the same direction.
A French trade mission then met with Canadian officials. This is not the first time that such Franco-Canadian trade talks have been held. Indeed they may become a more or less regular event. While our trade with France is not very large, it is, I believe, capable of expansion and the discussions this year were concerned with how this could best be done. We have been particularly impressed by the growing interest of France in the Canadian market.
Finally came informal discussions with a New Zealand trade delegation led by Hon. C. M. Bowden. Like other sterling area countries, New Zealand has been imposing very strict limitations on imports from Canada and other dollar countries. During the talks with Mr. Bowden, it was evident that New Zealand shares our interest in the restoration of normal trade relationships, and that there is more likelihood of progress in that direction now than for some time.
Another evidence of the government's continuing interest in trade was the decision to hold the Canadian international trade fair again in 1952. In many respects the fair held this year was the most successful since

the first fair was held in 1948. But the extent of participation by Canadian manufacturers and industrialists is disappointing. Furthermore, there is a good deal of uncertainty about the effects of defence preparations upon trade. In deciding to hold a fair next year the government is taking some risks. But, on the other hand, to abandon the fair this year might have been taken as evidence that the government no longer attaches the same importance to the development of trade, which would have had unfortunate repercussions at home and abroad. Whether the fair will continue beyond 1952 depends upon the extent to which Canadian businessmen take advantage of the opportunity provided to sell their wares not only abroad but to their neighbours at home.
In brief, Mr. Chairman, the Department of Trade and Commerce is continuing to take an active interest in the promotion of Canada's trade.

Mr. Chairman, I know that there was a good deal of disappointment over this year's Canadian international trade fair because of the lack of participation by Canadian manufacturers. I visited the fair on more than one occasion and was certainly distressed, to put it mildly, to see the lack of interest which our own manufacturers displayed in the fair. One would have hoped that this trade fair would have been the beginning of international trade with the rest of the world by Canada, and particularly those nations with whom we did not normally trade before the war. The pattern of trade that we are going to see in the years to come may be, and probably will be, very different from the old triangular pattern of trade that we saw prior to the war. At that time we were more or less the sterling broker for the United Kingdom and the United States.
I was surprised to find the lack of interest, and I may say rather disappointed, because I had hoped that this trade fair would have opened up an opportunity for the exhibition of the goods that we had to sell to the countries that are just emerging from the aftermath of the war and the currency and other restrictions imposed by war conditions. The foreign countries, particularly Holland, Italy, and to a degree Germany, had an excellent exhibit. The machine tool exhibit I thought was in every way admirable, but the fair this year seemed to be lacking something. Whether it was a disbelief in world trade, or whether it was some degree of disenchantment of the Canadian manufacturer with the
Supply-Trade and Commerce outlook, I do not know. But certainly we have no cause for satisfaction over the present situation.
Things are difficult. The problem of currency, the problem of exchange, is a besetting evil that is destroying today all attempts at international trade, and I hope that will be the subject of debate in this house at another time; but it seemed to me, Mr. Chairman, that there was a lack of appreciation of Canada's opportunity at the present time to open out in new markets. I just wonder whether the minister would care to comment on what must be to him, and the officials who worked so hard at this fair, a rather disappointing situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I would not say that the fair this year was disappointing. In many ways I think it was the best fair that we have held. However, if the fair suffered from anything it suffered from the fact that it was being held in a seller's market. Practically everything that was on exhibit at the fair was sold on the first day of the fair, and anyone capable of taking orders had his order book filled very early.
The department is concerned about the lack of interest by Canadian exhibitors. Very serious consideration was given to making this year's fair the last, but we had such a strong protest from the Toronto board of trade and from other business organizations across Canada, particularly from people who did not exhibit in the fair itself, we decided to continue the fair for one more year with the distinct warning that if there is no increase in Canadian participation in 1952, 1952 will be the last trade fair.

The minister has spoken
about trade with certain European countries. I want to raise a question regarding trade with China, because within the last few days I have received an air mail letter from what I believe to be a responsible organization in Hong Kong, known as the China Coast Navigating and Engineering Officers Guild. So far as I know it is an organization consisting of officers of the merchant marine of commonwealth countries.
In this letter the general secretary points out that there are certain vessels belonging to the Ming Sung Company, a company that I believe has its offices in Montreal, because I took the trouble to look up the directory and I found that it was registered there. It is claimed that certain ships of this company are trading between Hong Kong and Macao, where they are carrying passengers and cargo, between Hong Kong. Macao and

Supply-Trade and Commerce Canton, which would be of course a triangular line, again carrying passengers and cargo, and between Hong Kong and Canton, where they are carrying cargoes only.
I understand that these ships are ships which were built in Canada and were to be sold to the central Chinese government before that government fell, and that now they are operating out of Hong Kong under a Canadian flag, and still with Canadian registry, and that the government derives some revenue from this operation. Canton of course is a port which is under direct control of a government which has not been recognized by the Canadian government, and is to all intents and purposes a government with which we are in active warlike operations in Korea.
What cargoes are these vessels carrying? I ask that question because, according to the letter I have, and I quote:
Eye witnesses state that included in the daily cargoes is essential war material.
Of course if that is a fact it is something which will be very distressing to a great many people in Canada. I am told that the merchant naval officers associations, both in Canada and in Hong Kong, are seriously perturbed over this situation. There is no doubt that the letter states that these vessels are trading under the Canadian flag and have it painted prominently on both sides. The letter says that they wear the Canadian ensign in Chinese communist ports. These vessels are officered and manned by Chinese, and in one case there is- a Russian captain, according to the information. Without going into it in more detail at the present time I wonder whether the minister has any information about that situation, and if he can tell us whether there is any trade going on between Hong Kong and communist China by ships of Canadian registry or carrying the Canadian flag?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
These ships were built in
Canada by an arrangement that was current post-war, by which private transactions between Canadian firms and Chinese firms, or firms of other countries, could be carried out with the guarantee of both governments guaranteeing the loan. The Ming Sung Company came here and made a contract with two or three Canadian shipyards. They had a guarantee of the then government of China, and the loan was jointly guaranteed by the then government of China and the government of Canada. The ships were sold in the ordinary way through a commercial transaction, and the ships passed to the flag


of China, subject to a mortgage held by the Canadian shipyard and deposited with the bank that lent the money.
All went well until the Chinese government, the government of Chiang Kai-shek, fell, and then the banks began to worry a little about their loan. In the uncertain situation that followed, it seemed wise to transfer the ships to the Canadian flag, which was done at the request of the Ming Sung Company, which expressed a desire to protect their loans in Canada. I may say that the loans in Canada are not in default at the moment. The payments have been made when due. I do not know the outstanding balance, but while there are substantial balances there is no default in the loan. However, it is a fact that the ships are operating under the Canadian flag. The government is not happy about it. The operation of the ships is supervised by the government of Hong Kong which, as my hon. friend knows, is also a British colony. Whether the ships are carrying contraband in their trips to Canton and up the Yangtze river I cannot say. I hope they are not. If they are-well, I do not know what we could do about it. While they are Canadian flag ships they are not in any way subject to the direction of the Canadian government.
They are not owned by the Canadian government. We can withdraw the flag, and that is about all we can do. But the government has no direct interest in the situation other than that they are guarantor to a Canadian bank for part of the money that built the ships for the Ming Sung Company.

If these ships are sailing under the Canadian flag would not the government of Canada be responsible for seeing that these ships were manned according to the Canada Shipping Act, that they had officers of Canadian nationality or at least carrying Canadian certificates? Could not the certificates be withdrawn from the ships' officers if they are not carrying out the other regulations?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am sorry to say that is not the situation. When the flag was transferred the ships were exempted from the shipping regulations which required them to be officered by Canadians.
When they came back under the Canadian flag would they not then have to conform to the Canadian shipping regulations?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
When they came back under the Canadian flag they were exempted from the requirements. This was the most disturbing condition to meet and, rather than let the ships go, which might have been

the wisest course, we did take what seemed to be the practical course, to bring the physical ships under the Canadian flag, but to exempt the ships from the requirements of the Canada Shipping Act as long as they operated in Chinese waters.

I had no idea that these ships were carrying out operations right into the heart of China, up the Yangtze river. That is the first time I had heard about it. I did not know they were still operating into the heart of Red China. It is inconceivable that they are not carrying material there which would be very useful for the prosecution of the war by Red China-and our Canadian boys today are fighting against Red China up in Korea. . I cannot help thinking that the government must take some firmer action, even if it had to confiscate those ships. It seems to me an appalling situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: How would we confiscate them? Would we send the army up the Yangtze to take them over? That is about the only way we could get our hands on them, I think.
No. If they are operating out of Hong Kong, that is a long way from the Yangtze river. We have Canadian destroyers in those waters now. Perhaps those Canadian destroyers could do something about it.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am informed that the two on the Yangtze river have been seized by the communists, and they are operated by the communists. They may or may not carry the flag. I doubt very much if they carry the Canadian flag. I think those two ships that have been seized are carrying the communist flag. The others are operating out of Hong Kong and we are assured by the Hong Kong officials that they are not carrying contraband.
How many ships are there?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: There are five ships, two others have been seized by the communists.
There are two up the Yangtze, making up the original seven?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Yes.
1 think it is a pretty sorry situation.
Where are they registered? What is their home port-Vancouver or Montreal?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am sorry, but I cannot say.
Toronto.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It might easily be Toronto.

It might, at that.
Supply-Trade and Commerce

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
And they are not my problem,
I should say. I had nothing to do with them, except that when they got into difficulty I was called in to try to straighten out the trouble. But they have nothing to do with my department, I am happy to say.
I think the minister said there are mortgages on the ships. Would it not be possible to have them seized and sold under those mortgages in Hong Kong, and in that way clean up this mess?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It might not be the right thing to do. The Department of External Affairs and the Department of Finance are struggling with the situation. 1 should not be talking about it at all, because I know very little about it, and I have nothing to do with it.
Have we any check on the cargoes taken out on these ships? We have a trade commissioner, have we not, in Hong Kong? Has he any responsibility in the matter?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The Hong Kong government is responsible for checking cargo in and out of Hong Kong, and I am sure they do it efficiently. As I say, with respect to the two ships up the Yangtze, I make no promises about them.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The two ships up the Yangtze are down the river.

We have two good dollar markets, one in Cuba and one in Venezuela. What is being done to increase our trade with those two countries? We used to ship our maritime products to Cuba. We have lost most of that trade on account of the duties. Venezuela is the only South American country which is a dollar market. They have been taking a lot of produce, including potatoes, from the maritime provinces lately. I was wondering what is being done to increase trade with Venezuela.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We have a large and growing trade with Venezuela, of which I hope to have the figures in a moment. We are doing everything we can to give that market good service, and I think our relations are most cordial.
The trade is growing there?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The trade is growing every year, yes. Exports to Venezuela in 1947 were $12,988,625; in 1948,	$16,934,563;	1949,
$27,688,637; and 1950, $25,456,741.
Our imports from Venezuela in 1947 were $46 million; 1948, $94 million; 1949, $91 million and 1950, $87 million. The imports of course from Venezuela are chiefly of oil. So it should be a good market for Canada because the balance of trade is in favour of Venezuela.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
So far as Cuba is concerned, our trade relations there should be considerably better because of our agreement to take 75,000 short tons of sugar annually from that country.

I have wondered whether it would be possible for me to get the general picture of the functions of the Department of Trade and Commerce. It is a department, we must admit, that does a good deal of work. I am wondering what its general aims are. I might commence questioning to obtain the information I want by asking the minister what was the purpose of holding the international trade fair in Toronto. Was it to enable Canadian producers to sell more Canadian goods abroad, or was it to enable Canada to buy more goods from abroad?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
It was to set up a marketplace where goods from Canada and goods from abroad could be displayed and purchased either by Canadians or by foreign buyers, as the circumstances might permit. The purpose was to assist exports and to assist Canadian buyers in selecting imports. One distinct purpose it has achieved is in putting our manufacturers on their toes. They have seen displayed the best products of a great number of countries abroad and I think they are making better articles as a result of seeing what the competition is in foreign markets.
The difficulty in offering Canadian goods for sale abroad is the currency restrictions. We hope that they are moving toward the end of currency restrictions and if that should happen I am sure there will be greater Canadian participation in the fair. I believe the fair has served a useful purpose. When there was talk of closing it up this year we received protests in a volume that really surprised me. The future of the fair is not too definite. We will try it one more year and if we get greater Canadian participation we will try to make it a permanent feature. Otherwise I think perhaps we may wind it up.

Are there officials in the department whose duty it is to look over the broad field 'to decide what is best for Canada? We in Canada are capable of producing certain goods to our advantage, and it is to our advantage to sell certain goods abroad. What goods would it pay us to produce and sell abroad, and what goods would it not be in the best interests of the Canadian economy to produce and sell abroad? What goods could we buy advantageously from abroad? If questions like that were asked it seems to me that we would have an over-all purpose in mindi.
In order to illustrate what I have in mind I shall refer to something which I have talked


about in this house from time to time for fifteen years-beet sugar. I do not propose to discuss sugar beets, I simply refer to them . as an illustration. It is well known that the production of beet sugar enriches the land and it enables us to feed livestock to advantage. It provides a number of advantages to Canadian economy which are not given by many manufactures.
Are there commodities which Canada could produce which would benefit the Canadian economy generally in the way much as the beet sugar industry does? Would it not be wise for us to single out such commodities and aim to sell them rather than to sell such commodities as zinc, copper, lead and other base metals which actually permanently deplete our resources? If we expand the sale of such commodities overmuch our grandchildren will find in this country a pile of rocks instead of a great heritage passed on to them.
It seems to me that we have reached the point in our national life where considerations of this sort ought to be rather prominent in our thinking. I am trying to bring matters down to a focus so that the minister will have some chance of answering. Are we going too far in exporting wood pulp, for instance? Are we selling so much wood pulp abroad that we are depleting our forests beyond the point to which we should deplete them? Are we selling fish abroad to the extent where we are tending to deplete our fish resources? Has the department consciously contemplated these things generally and, if so, what has been the result of the departmental thinking?
Have they decided what commodities we can afford to export? It is quite obvious that if we continue to produce wheat and sell it abroad, sooner or later we are going to deplete the fertility of our soil. If that goes on too far then the great-grandchildren of this generation will find themselves in a country no longer rich as it once was. That is what will happen unless we take some measures to restore the fertility of our soil now being exhausted by the production of crops like wheat, oats and barley for export abroad.
Has the minister's department given conscious thought to matters such as these? After the minister finishes with these questions I am going to ask if the department has given conscious thought to the things we ought to be importing rather than producing at home.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
As I see it, the function of the Department of Trade and Commerce is to find markets for any surpluses Canada may have. It has never been the purpose of the

department to tell Canadians what they should produce. It is the function of the department to dispose of any production that is surplus over home requirements. For that purpose we maintain offices in almost every country of the world and have there aggressive representatives who find markets for anything that we have, as surplus.
My hon. friend has suggested that we should plan our economy, but as an illustration he chose a most unfortunate item. A great many countries of the world produce sugar from beets, but I do not know of any beet sugar from any country that moves into the export market. Sugar beets have the geographical advantage that they can be grown where the sugar is consumed. Their production is beneficial to the soil although I think my hon. friend will agree that it is hard on the labour that produces the beets. It is not an easy matter to grow sugar beets and harvest them. Nevertheless, it is a good domestic crop. This industry is being kept healthy by duties against cane sugar and by any other help the government can give.
I cannot agree that we should keep our metals in the ground. It is through the mining of metals that the waste spaces of Canada have been populated and made prosperous. I do not suppose there would be much of a settlement around Kimberley except for the mining that is carried on there, and I am sure that there would not be much of a settlement around Sudbury or Flin Flon were it not for the mines in those areas. Canada is a country of varying resources and each district is made possible by the exploitation of some natural resource that can be produced in surplus.

Apparently the Department of Trade and Commerce looks upon itself more or less as a clearing house; it does not aim to give leadership or guidance to the nation in respect of products which it. would be valuable to the nation to produce or import. The department merely takes what is produced and endeavours to dispose of it to best advantage. I do not know whether it will be in order to ask the minister this question as it may be considered to be an unfair question. I wonder if the minister does not think that somewhere in Canada we ought to have an organization thinking in terms of the future. The minister says that we have to exploit our resources, and of course I know what he means. It would not benefit us to keep all our minerals in the ground, but nevertheless I think the minister will grant, without any argument at all, that it is an exceedingly unwise procedure to exhaust the minerals in any given area. For example, it is conceivable that Sudbury might 80709-263
Supply-Trade and Commerce become a ghost town in due time, and Kimberley might become a ghost town. The question will have to -be raised some time before it is too late as to how many towns we can afford to build up and then allow to become ghosts.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I might suggest there are ministries that have the job to which my friend has referred. For instance, we have a Minister of Agriculture and the Department of Agriculture. Their duty is to keep the agricultural industry of Canada healthy, and each province has an agricultural department for the same purpose. The same is true of mining. We have a minister of mines and each province has a minister of mines, their duty being to make sure that the mineral assets of the country are properly harvested. In the same way the forests belong to the provinces, and each province has a minister of forests. We have a department of government that has general oversight over forests from the dominion's point of view. The work of planning the use of Canada's resources is handled, but it is not handled by the Department of Trade and Commerce. That is the point I am making. I would not like my hon. friend to think I was implying that the job was not being done.
That is what I wanted to know.
I should like to ask the minister what significance he attaches to the present price war in the United States. Does he see it spreading to Canada?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: As far as I understand the situation, they had fair trade laws in the United States which provided that if a contract was made between the producer of a proprietary article and one distributor, the price stated in that contract applied to all distributors in the area. That law was set aside by one of the high courts of the United States with the result that certain department stores undertook special sales of these proprietary articles that they were free to mark down for the first time. That developed into price competition. It was perhaps speeded up owing to the fact that department store sales were off anyway, and there was a desire to clear stock and speed up distribution through department stores. I hardly think it is a big enough affair to be called a war. It was a skirmish between four or five' or six large department stores in the city of New York. I think it has hardly spread outside that area, and I think it has no great significance in the over-all economic situation.
You do not see it approaching Canada at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
No.

Supply-Trade and Commerce

In view of the great industrial development of the west, would the minister consider staging the great trade fair in the west next year having in mind the manufacturing that takes place in Vancouver, Seattle, Los Angeles and elsewhere along the Pacific coast, and the fact that we are now reviving trade with Japan, South America, and so on? Perhaps by next year there may be peace in the Pacific, and the trade fair could be very well staged some place in British Columbia. It would give the mining people particularly an opportunity in the same way that the aluminum people have taken very good advantage of the opportunity to exhibit at Toronto. I want to congratulate the department on staging the fair. I have attended it on two occasions. I find it is a tremendous emporium, and I am sure the bringing together of these people from all these nations with their exhibits and merchandise is of tremendous assistance towards world peace. I should like to see it staged in Vancouver.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I am sure my officers will take note of the hon. member's remarks.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Could we not reserve our remarks on fairs and exhibitions until we reach items 455 and 456?

Can the minister tell us the trend of Canada's trade balance in 1951? I was quite struck by a little publication entitled "Business Review" issued by the Bank of Montreal under date of May 23, 1951. They say in part:
... a closer analysis- of last year's external transactions, viewed in conjunction with trade trends thus far in 1951, reveals some significant changes that flash a light of warning against an overly complacent attitude toward this country's position on international account.
Dealing with the 1951 position in so far as merchandise trading between Canada and the United States is concerned they say:
In merchandise trading transactions, the early months of 1951 have witnessed an abrupt reversal of the former welcome contraction of our deficit with the United States and a correspondingly sharp accentuation of the unfavourable trend in our overall balance. While average monthly shipments across the border in the first quarter of this year were about 5 per cent higher in value than throughout 1950, imports were up by 30 per cent. Thus the trade deficit with the U.S.A. in the three months to the end of March-
That is the present year.
*-was about $140 millions, as contrasted with only $47 millions for the whole of last year. The value of merchandise moving across the seas in both directions has shown little significant change. The consequence is that Canadian merchandise trade with all countries, which resulted in a reduced but still favourable balance of $10 millions in the full year 1950, has shown an unfavourable balance of $124 millions in the first quarter of 1951.


The statement indicates that the unfavourable balance with the United States is a great deal higher in the first three months of 1951 than it was last year, and also that our unfavourable balance with regard to the world at large is a great deal higher than it was in 1950. Can the minister tell us whether or not these figures are correct and, if so, whether that trend has continued through April and May?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The figures are quite correct. Our trade with the United States is out of balance through abnormal imports from the United States. Our exports to the United States are running at a record level, considerably higher than at any former time in history. But with the purchase of war materials from that country, which have been coming in in volume, and the tremendous capital investment program going on in Canada, which exceeds by far any previous record, we have been buying materials from the United States in excess of normal purchases. Aside from that the balance has not changed greatly. Our trade with Great Britain is in about the same balance as it was last year, and also our trade with the sterling area. Trade with South America has grown greatly but it is in fair balance. The balance has hot changed much. Any change that has taken place is in our trade with the United States and is the result of greatly expanded imports from that country. I believe that this situation is abnormal. We are in a strong financial position to stand it, and I think it can be straightened out when our building boom settles down. The economic measures we have taken to check capital expansion in the country are designed to check the very circumstances my friend has called to my attention.
Does the minister think that on merchandising transactions between Canada and the United States there will be a greater deficit this year than in 1950?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Oh, yes; very much greater.
Canada's position will be a great deal worse -this year than it was last year, oh those transactions?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It will be further out of balance; in other words there will be a greater deficit in our account with the United States, and probably a deficit in our account with the world. The reason for that, of course, is our large investment program. My hon. friend will appreciate that as more of Canada's production is invested at home less becomes available for export, and the greater the pressure for increased imports.

I am interested in this because our adverse balance of trade at the present time with all countries is running about half a billion dollars a year. I would like the minister to enlarge on that. He has said this is largely due to capital expenditures.
I gather, from talking with manufacturers I know and from the press, that up to the present time defence orders placed in Canada by the United States have been extremely disappointing, and that so far there has been very little reciprocal business in defence equipment and defence material as between the two countries. I wonder if the minister would care to comment on that.
Then I have seen members of his department at work in various fields. I saw some of his trade commissioners in Germany, and I believe the work our trade commissioners are doing, under great difficulties, deserves the highest commendation. But each man I spoke to told me in one way or another that his principal difficulty and in fact his only difficulty in selling Canadian goods was currency control. There was no question that the goods we were producing in Canada, whether raw materials or finished products, were desirable and of the type required, but in country after country they could not import them over the barrier of currency control. Perhaps the minister would say a word on those two points, first the lack of reciprocal business in defence purchases by the United States and the difficulties in regard to currency restrictions.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I have no particular complaint to make as far as defence purchasing is concerned. The Americans were able to sell us certain war materials off the shelf, you might say, or out of stock; and those materials have been moving. We have had nothing to sell back in the way of war materials off the shelf, though we have taken contracts which will be productive as our production steps up and the goods are delivered. The contracts on both sides are not in balance, but there is a tendency for them to come into balance. I am not particularly worried about the upset in exchange due to war business between the two countries; I believe that situation will straighten out if there is the will to straighten it out, and I think everyone is doing his best along that line. I was just looking at the trade figures for the first three months, and in our account with the United States there was a deficit of $100 million, which is very close to the amount of our deficit with the world. Well, that is not too serious. If it continues at that rate during the year we will have a deficit of $400 million, and that is not anything to worry about. We have had far greater deficits. In 1947 we were losing a billion dollars a year to the United States.
Supply-Trade and Commerce However, that is a trend we do not like, but we think it is a trend that can be reversed whenever we are willing to curtail our investment program and cut down on abnormal purchasing in the United States.
Would the minister care to say anything about currency difficulties?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The currency difficulties are improving. Every time we bring trade with any country into balance we make it possible for them to relax the restrictions. In most countries with which Canada is accustomed to trade, restrictions are being relaxed to some extent. They are not being relaxed as quickly as we think they should be, but we are constantly pressing for the relaxation of restrictive measures. Some progress is being made, and we think the trend is in the right direction.

It seems to me a number of hon. members speak of these currency restrictions as though they had been imposed as a sort of punitive measure, instead of being something imposed through necessity. If a nation finds itself importing more goods than it is exporting, one of the most effective devices to prevent that sort of thing is to control foreign exchange, which means currency restrictions. It is quite idle to talk about removing currency restrictions unless first we do as the minister says; that is, unless we manage to enable the country concerned to sell us as much goods as it buys, or to balance its trade in a three-way arrangement. So it seems to me we are rather more optimistic than we should be if we think this matter of currency restrictions will more or less iron itself out. As long as we do not buy enough goods from Britain, for example, to enable her to buy the goods we wish to sell her, Britain will have to use quotas or currency restrictions against us in defence of her own economy.
I would like to hear a little discussion along that line. This was all involved at the time of the Bretton Woods discussion. Many hon. members seemed to think all we had to do was clamp on the restrictions envisaged by Bretton Woods and all difficulties would right themselves. That has not happened, however; now we find that they had the cart before the horse, and there seems to be quite a bit of uncertainty as to what should be done. This was one of the considerations that caused me to ask the minister the questions I put to him in the beginning. I was wondering whether it would be wise to manage the Canadian economy in such a way that we could buy from Britain the goods we need to buy in order to enable her to purchase the wheat and other commodities we desire to sell, or whether it would be wise

Supply-Trade and Commerce lor us to envisage a more or less closed economy, or a balanced economy, or a selfsufficient economy in Canada and use some other means to enable Britain to buy the goods we want her to buy from us, something similar to the mutual aid device we used during the war.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I am happy to say that we
finished 1950 with an adverse trade balance with the rest of the sterling area. In other words the rest of the sterling area sold us more goods than we sold them. There was a slight balance in our favour with the United Kingdom, as between the two countries, but it was very much smaller than ever before and showed a gap that presents no particular problem. As far as the balance of trade between Canada and any sterling area country is concerned, however, there is no good reason why the barriers cannot be taken down, and we think they should be taken down much faster than that is being done.

That is, the barriers
between the various countries of the sterling area, but not the barriers between the sterling area and the dollar area?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The sterling area and Canada. As I say, the sterling area sold us more than we sold to the sterling area, that is including England as part of the sterling area.

I think the minister is to be congratulated now on bringing about this dollar situation. A few years ago we used to hear a lot in this house about our trade being on a triangular basis. We bought far more from the United States than we sold, and consequently we had to sell more to Europe and insist upon payment in dollars in order to use those dollars to make up our deficit with the United States. Consequently, as a result of that policy Europe did try to impose heavy restrictions upon trade with us in order to prevent having an unfavourable balance of trade with this country. I think the situation is far more satisfactory now. We are balancing our trade with the sterling area and trying, at the same time, to balance our trade with the United States. In other words, we are trying to increase our sales to the United States and increase our imports from the sterling area. I believe that is as it should be. If we continue that policy, I believe Europe will be willing to give up the restrictions against this country.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Item agreed to.
450. Commodities and allocations, including assistance in the development of markets and new industry, the procurement of supplies, and contributions as detailed in the estimates, $596,973.

This item 450 is an item that puts a question into my mind. It contains the phrase, "including assistance in the development of markets and new industry . . ." That is the phrase which a while ago made me ask the minister if he actually was consciously endeavouring to develop new industry in Canada. If he is not, then what is the purpose of having that phrase in that item? If the purpose is to develop new industry, what new industry and why?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The commodities and allocation branch is the office which indirectly supports the trade commissioners in the field. For instance, we have specialists in almost every type of production and raw materials. We have textile specialists, livestock specialists and so on, specialists in almost every product that Canada produces in surplus. These men meet the producers in Canada, and work out their problems with them. They communicate the instructions to our trade commissioners abroad. It is the Canadian end of the trade commissioners' service. I think that is a fair way of putting it.

I do not wish to be critical of the minister. I believe the minister has done a magnificent job ever since he began being a minister in this country. I have told him that several times before now. But I was wondering whether or not the minister was doing the same thing for civilian production that he obviously is doing for defence production. In his fine report earlier today, he indicated quite clearly that if he finds a deficiency of any particular commodity in Canada, he goes out consciously and gets that commodity. If he has to arrange to lend money to a company to produce the commodity or give the company special depreciation, he does it.
Now then, is the minister doing a similar thing with respect to civilian production? If he is, then I should like to know what civilian production he has in mind; what he is doing, and what success he is attaining. All these matters, as the minister fully knows, are involved in Canada's supply position. If we do not keep up and improve the supply position of Canada with respect to civilian consumer goods, then we are likely to be in a bad way.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
We do perhaps the job my hon. friend has in mind for industry. We point out opportunities abroad for a certain type of manufacture, and we send over the specifications to be filled. For instance, we point out to them there is an opportunity for longsleeved underwear in China or Japan or some part of the world. We send over the specifications, and find a market for the goods produced accordingly. We give industry all

the guidance that they will accept as to the the manufacture of goods suitable for certain specific markets.
I pointed out that it is not the duty of the department to do the same job for other types of production because they have separate ministries responsible for that chore, such as agriculture, fisheries, mines and other resources of the country. They have other ministries doing the same job.

That is about as it should be, but I am wondering if the Department of Trade and Commerce takes leadership over the other departments. Wheat is an example. I do not desire to discuss wheat, but wheat is primarily an agricultural matter. At the same time, it comes under the Department of Trade and Commerce, which has a considerable voice in respect of the wheat situation in Canada. I would think it would have a voice in any agreement to be negotiated.
Now then, when it comes to developing agricultural or forest products, is there an understanding or co-ordination between the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the other ministers so as to obtain an over-all picture of what we ought to get, and a decision as to what ought to be done?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: I may point out that wheat is a good example. The Department of Trade and Commerce has the job of marketing surplus Canadian wheat. The department has nothing to do with the amount of wheat that is grown; the variety that is grown or how it is planted or harvested; that is a matter for the Department of Agriculture. The marketing of the surplus is the job of the Department of Trade and Commerce, and it is because wheat is a surplus commodity that the marketing of wheat is in the Department of Trade and Commerce.

May I ask one more question about that long-sleeved underwear? The minister has said he will point out to the producers of underwear in Canada that there is a market in China or Japan for longsleeved underwear. I wonder whether or not he will go so far as to give financial support to a company which would enable it to produce long-sleeved underwear, much as he would give financial support to a company producing a particular kind of ship for defence. Would he give accelerated depreciation to a company to enable it to go into the production of this particular commodity for which he found a market?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The Department of Trade and Commerce has very little to do with money.
Supply-Trade and Commerce We have no money. If anyone wants money, we send him to the Department of Finance. Trade and commerce is simply a service department with particular responsibility for exports and imports.

But trade and commerce, in seeking to obtain a particular item of defence production, does have the determining voice as to whether or not financial assistance will be rendered to the company engaged in the production of that commodity, does it not?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
No; the Department of Trade
and Commerce is out of the defence business-it should never have been in it. Today defence business is the duty of the Department of Defence Production, which is quite different from the Department of Trade and Commerce.

Then the Department of
Defence Production does have a determining voice as to whether financial assistance shall be offered to a company that would be engaged in producing commodities.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Producing defence products.

What I am probing for
is to see whether or not there is something resembling a department of civilian production.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No.

It is not any part of the
function of the Department of Trade and Commerce to engage in that sort of activity?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: No.

It looks as if we ought
to have an organization that should do something like that before long in Canada.

The minister mentioned
that wheat was a surplus commodity. Can he tell the committee how much surplus of the various grades of wheat we have at the present time?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
At the present time we have
sold all that we dare to sell of grades one to five. We have a fair quantity of No. 6 wheat, and a fair quantity of feed wheat, but not too good. We hope that the whole situation will clear up shortly after the end of the crop year.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
May I point out
that there will be ample opportunity to discuss wheat when we reach items 464 and 465. Shall this item carry?

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Item agreed to.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Supply-Trade and Commerce
451. Trade commissioner service, including payment of compensation to trade commissioners for damage to and loss of furniture and effects, under regulations approved by the governor in council, $1,963,751.

Can the minister give us
any idea as to how our trade position is with the South American countries? Has it improved or deteriorated?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
The volume of our trade has
gone up very greatly, both exports and imports, and the improvement in the balance is favourable to Canada.

Have the trade commissioners abroad diplomatic privileges or not? I mention this because it is rather a sore point with some of them. The employees of the department of immigration, who in many cases are doing a great deal of extremely hard work under very difficult circumstances, do not enjoy diplomatic privileges, but some trade commissioners do enjoy diplomatic privileges. One or two suggested to me they wished that they all did have them. Is there any general agreement on this, or is there any general rule about whether they enjoy diplomatic privileges or not?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: If a trade commissioner is attached to an embassy he does enjoy diplomatic privileges. If there is no embassy in the country he is serving he does not have diplomatic privileges. Sometimes we try to get external affairs to give him consular status, which carries with it diplomatic privileges, but there are trade commissioners who do not have diplomatic privileges, and there seems to be no way in which diplomatic privileges can be obtained for them.

I must say that the granting of diplomatic privileges to a trade commissioner is of tremendous advantage to him and is of tremendous advantage to the country. If the minister could persuade his colleague, the Secretary of State for External Affairs, to grant diplomatic privileges to these trade commissioners it would be of great advantage to all concerned.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
Under the details of the trade commissioner service the figures -are given as to the expenses of each of the various offices. I realize that there are bound to be substantial differences in regard to these offices, but would the minister explain why, for instance, the trade commissioner service at Caracas is $77,877, and the trade commissioner's office at Melbourne is $24,335? I would like to have some indication as to what considerations result in so much larger expenditure in the office at Caracas than in the office at Melbourne. I simply take them as an illustration.
[The Deputy Chairman.]

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: The trade commissioners are paid a basic pay, as though they lived in Ottawa, and there are supplements, depending on the cost of living in the posts to which they are assigned. Caracas has the highest cost of living in the world, as far as I know. It has that record in the trade commissioners' service. On the other hand, the cost of living in Melbourne is probably no higher than the cost of living in Ottawa. It may be a bit, but I would believe that it was not much higher than in Ottawa.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I am taking such places as Wellington and Melbourne as places within the commonwealth where one would think the activities would be important, and then comparing them with such a place as Caracas, and for instance Manila, where the expenditures are $49,542, as compared with $20,466 in Wellington. Are the activities of these offices in the cities in the commonwealth not more important than they are in Manila or Caracas?

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: Well, the trade commissioners in these areas cover many countries. I suppose the trade commissioner in Caracas covers three or four other countries. He may have a larger office than the office in Melbourne. The office in the Philippines has been newly established and a drive has been made, a very successful drive, to get a share of the Philippine business. We have done big business there. I dare say some extra pressure has been put on that office, and perhaps extra expenses incurred. The very fact that it is set up new may have something to do with it. There are three offices in Australia. The work is divided.
What are the qualifications for appointment of trade commissioners? To my mind he should foe a man who can sell Canada and Canada's products.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: They must be university graduates with some trade experience. Trade commissioners are taken into the service in a junior capacity, and put through a course of training which takes at least a year. The trade commissioner is sent to all parts of Canada. The first requirement is that he must know Canada and Canadian industry thoroughly. Then he is put in a junior position abroad, and gradually given the experience required to foe a trade commissioner.
